question: What is the primary definition of the route of transmission in epidemiology?

options.A: The genetic mutation rate of a pathogen
options.B: The specific pathway by which a pathogen moves from a source to a susceptible host
options.C: The time it takes for symptoms to appear after exposure
options.D: The classification of bacteria based on Gram-staining

explanation: The route of transmission specifically refers to the pathway that a pathogen takes to travel from a reservoir or source to a susceptible host. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why is understanding the route of transmission critical for clinical nurses?

options.A: It helps determine the correct PPE and isolation protocols to halt disease spread
options.B: It replaces the need for administering prescribed medications
options.C: It is only useful for laboratory technicians studying viruses
options.D: It dictates the exact financial cost of hospital stays

explanation: Knowing the transmission route allows nurses to implement targeted precautions, choose proper PPE, and enforce isolation protocols effectively. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h1)

question: What are the three core components of the Epidemiological Triangle?
explanation: The Epidemiological Triangle is composed of the agent, the host, and the environment interacting together. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h2)

question: How can an infection be stopped according to the Chain of Infection model?

options.B: By breaking any single link in the six-step chain
options.C: By ensuring all hosts have the same blood type
options.D: By removing the environmental temperature completely

explanation: An infection can be halted by breaking any single link within the six components of the Chain of Infection. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is required for direct contact transmission to take place?

options.B: Close physical proximity and touch between the source and a susceptible host
options.C: An insect vector such as a mosquito
options.D: Air currents moving across a large hospital ward

explanation: Direct contact transmission requires physical touch or close proximity allowing the pathogen to pass directly without an intermediary. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h3)

question: Which of the following pathogens is commonly transmitted via direct contact?

options.D: Influenza virus via wide air currents

explanation: MRSA is a classic example of an organism frequently spread through direct contact in healthcare and community settings. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is a fomite in the context of indirect contact transmission?

options.A: A living insect that carries a parasite
options.B: An inanimate object that becomes contaminated with pathogens
options.C: A microscopic droplet suspended in the air
options.D: A chemical disinfectant used on skin

explanation: A fomite refers to any inanimate object or surface that can harbor and transmit infectious agents. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which nursing action is most effective in preventing indirect contact transmission via fomites?

options.A: Using stethoscopes on multiple patients without cleaning them
options.B: Disinfecting medical equipment and practicing consistent hand hygiene
options.C: Avoiding all physical contact with hospital furniture
options.D: Keeping windows closed at all times

explanation: Properly disinfecting equipment and performing hand hygiene stops pathogens from being transferred via contaminated objects. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h4)

question: What is a key characteristic of droplet transmission compared to airborne transmission?

options.A: Droplets travel long distances and remain suspended for hours
options.B: Droplets are large, travel short distances (< 1 meter), and quickly settle
options.C: Droplets require negative pressure rooms for containment
options.D: Droplets only spread through contaminated blood products

explanation: Droplet transmission involves large particles that travel short distances and settle quickly, unlike airborne particles that remain suspended. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h5)

question: Which type of personal protective equipment is required when caring for a patient with an airborne disease like tuberculosis?

options.C: Particulate respirator such as an N95 mask
options.D: Plastic face shield without respiratory protection

explanation: Airborne precautions require specialized particulate respirators like N95 masks to filter out tiny suspended droplet nuclei. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h5)

question: What defines vector-borne transmission of infectious diseases?

options.A: The spread of pathogens through contaminated municipal water supplies
options.B: The transmission of pathogens through living organisms such as mosquitoes and ticks
options.C: The direct transfer of skin flora through handshakes
options.D: The inhalation of dust particles containing fungal spores

explanation: Vector-borne transmission relies on living arthropod vectors like mosquitoes and ticks to carry and transfer pathogens to humans. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which disease is a primary example of a vector-borne infection transmitted by mosquitoes in tropical regions?
explanation: Malaria is a classic vector-borne disease transmitted by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h6)

question: What characterizes common vehicle transmission?

options.A: A single contaminated source spreads a pathogen to multiple hosts simultaneously
options.B: Pathogens are spread exclusively through direct skin-to-skin touch
options.C: Infection occurs only through airborne droplets in confined spaces
options.D: Transmission relies entirely on insect vectors like fleas

explanation: Common vehicle transmission happens when one contaminated source, such as food or water, infects many people at once. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h7)

question: Which of the following is a key nursing responsibility in preventing bloodborne transmission?

options.A: Boiling drinking water before patient consumption
options.B: Verifying blood product safety and adhering to strict sharps safety protocols
options.C: Spraying hospital wards with general insecticides
options.D: Ensuring all food is served raw to preserve nutrients

explanation: Nurses prevent bloodborne transmission by strictly following sharps safety and double-checking blood products before transfusion. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of primary prevention interventions in community health nursing?

options.A: To treat chronic complications after a disease has fully developed
options.B: To stop disease before it occurs through education and vaccination
options.C: To trace contacts after an outbreak has already peaked
options.D: To disinfect hospital instruments after a surgical procedure

explanation: Primary prevention focuses on stopping diseases before they start using strategies like vaccination and health education. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h8)

question: How do community health nurses contribute to secondary prevention during an infectious disease outbreak?

options.A: By administering routine childhood immunizations only
options.B: By engaging in contact tracing, screening, and early case detection
options.C: By manufacturing new pharmaceutical drugs in laboratories
options.D: By designing municipal water treatment plants

explanation: Secondary prevention involves early detection, screening, and contact tracing to catch infections early and limit further spread. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h8)
